about: How a date is written and read, stated where both sides of the wire can be held to it.
What a date looks like belongs to whoever is logged in, and the server owns that preference —
an order and a separator, assembled into one PHP format string. The field in the browser is
handed that same string and has to write text the server will accept, and accept text the
server will write. So the rule is implemented twice, in two languages, and neither
implementation can see the other.
Drift between them is silent in the worst way. A spelling the browser writes and the server
refuses is a bound that vanishes out of a filter with nothing said; a spelling the server
accepts and the browser refuses is a field that reports somebody's own saved value as
unreadable. Neither raises anything at the moment it goes wrong.
Both sides hold themselves to one rule, stated the same way in each: a text is a date written
in a format only if writing that date back out under the same format reproduces the text. That
is what makes the cases below agree by construction rather than by two lists being kept in step
— padding, letter case and the spelling of a named month are all covered by it at once, and
neither side needs a list of the ways a token can be mis-typed.
It also keeps a token meaning what the format says. Left to its own devices PHP's parser reads
`9/3/2026` under `d/m/Y`, which would make `d` a second way of writing `j` and leave the
distinction the format draws unenforced. Under the round trip both sides refuse it, because
`d` writes `09`.
`writes` are round trips both sides must agree on: writing the instant under the format must
produce exactly that text, and reading that text back must return exactly that instant.
`refuses` must be refused by both, since a date half-understood is worse than one rejected.
`names` is the other half of the same agreement. A named month is not a translation either side
gets to make: PHP's date formatting ignores the locale — `F` answers "March" whether the locale
is French, German or Japanese — and `createFromFormat` reads back only these spellings, refusing
`mars`, `Mär` and `3月` alike. So the browser holds them as constants rather than being sent them,
and this is what holds the two lists to each other. Should either side ever start translating a
month, the field would show a name somebody recognises and then refuse to read it back; this is
what fails first instead. `daysMin` is the exception with only one side to it: no format token
writes it, so it is held to the columns a week is drawn in rather than to a written date.
`means` is the instant, written in `as` — the one spelling that does not vary and belongs to
no preference. A case naming no time is about a day, and is compared as one.
`machineFormats` is the other list neither side owns: the spellings a seeded value is tried
under once the format in force has been. A value is written by one side and read back by the
other, so a spelling only one of them tries is a saved value reported back as unreadable to
whoever saved it. The set is the agreement; the order is not, and no case pins one. Under the
round trip a shorter spelling cannot match a longer text — `Y-m-d` refuses `2026-03-09 15:05`
for the text left over — so trying them in any order answers the same.
`tokens` and `halves` are the second question both sides ask of a format, after how to spell
one date in it: which of the two halves it spells at all. That is what decides whether a
field draws a grid of days, a clock, or both — so where the two sides read a format
differently, one of them draws a control for something the other is not asking for, and the
field offers a day to fill in that will never be posted. `halves` covers what a token on its
own cannot: a backslash makes a letter of whatever follows it, and a letter is not a token.
`separators` is what the preference may put between the parts of a date. The browser splits
a format into its halves along them, so one the server can write and the browser does not
know leaves that punctuation stranded on a half it does not belong to.
